chief_complaint: high fever, night sweats, and new heart murmur in IV drug user
hpi_details: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with high fever, night sweats, and new heart murmur in iv drug user. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she has a persistent bout of the flu or a chest infection that her immune system cannot shake off.
concerns: She is worried she might have lymphoma because the drenching night sweats remind her of a close friend's cancer.
expectations: She hopes to receive a prescription for strong antibiotics and a blood test to clear the fever before the weekend.

investigation_events.title: Blood culture results
investigation_events.availability_message: The blood culture results are now available.

results.value: Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus isolated from all 3 sets

investigation_events.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: Mobile 16 x 8 mm vegetation on the tricuspid valve with moderate tricuspid regurgitation

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infective Endocarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management requires urgent hospital evaluation, three blood-culture sets before antibiotics when feasible, and echocardiography (usually transthoracic first, followed by transesophageal imaging when indicated); empiric antibiotics should follow culture collection and local infectious-disease guidance.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: high fever, night sweats, and new heart murmur in IV drug user

Key HPI features: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with high fever, night sweats, and new heart murmur in iv drug user. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infective Endocarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Occult malignancy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New heart failure, stroke, or embolic phenomena.
management_principles: Urgently admit, obtain three blood-culture sets before antibiotics when feasible, obtain transthoracic echocardiography followed by transesophageal imaging when indicated, and begin empiric antibiotics using local infectious-disease guidance
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Infection of a heart valve. Fever plus a new murmur is the pairing that must not be missed, and the history hunts for a source.
red_flags: New heart failure, stroke, or embolic phenomena

must_ask.say: How long have you had the fevers?
Have you been sweating at night or losing weight?
Do you have any known heart valve problem or a prosthetic valve?

must_ask.objective: Source — dental work, procedures, IV drug use
must_ask.say: Have you had dental treatment, a procedure, or do you inject any drugs?
Any sudden weakness, vision problems, or painful lumps on your fingers?
How far can you walk on the flat before you need to stop?

history.answer: I have had a high fever and drenching night sweats for the past five days, and I feel completely exhausted.
The high fever started about five days ago and has been gradually getting worse every single day.
My temperature reached 39.2 degrees at home yesterday, and the fever comes with severe shaking chills followed by heavy sweating.
I tried taking ibuprofen two days ago, but it only brought my fever down for a couple of hours before it spiked again.
No, I haven't had any cough, phlegm, or sore throat at all.
I feel a bit winded when I walk up stairs or carry groceries, which is completely new for me.
No, I don't have any pain or burning when I urinate, no frequent urination, and no flank pain.
No stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; my appetite is just lower than usual.
I have a mild dull headache with the fever, but no severe sudden headache, stiff neck, or confusion.
No, I haven't noticed any unusual skin rashes, black bug bite scabs, or swollen painful joints.
I've had severe night sweats every night this week where I wake up drenched, and I think I've lost about two kilograms over the past two weeks.
No, I haven't felt any lumps or swollen glands in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I have not traveled abroad, gone hiking in tall grass, or handled farm animals recently.
No one around me is sick or running a fever.
No, I have never had chemotherapy and I do not take steroids or any immune system medications.
I have never had any heart murmurs, valve problems, or rheumatic fever, and I haven't had any dental work or surgical procedures recently.
No, I haven't started taking any new prescription drugs or herbal products.
I inject heroin intravenously into my arm veins, mostly about twice a week, and I last injected three days ago using equipment that might have been shared.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my long-term partner and haven't had any new sexual contacts.
No, I haven't seen any painful red bumps on my fingertips, spots on my palms or soles, or bleeding under my nails.
I thought I just caught a nasty strain of the flu or a chest bug that my body can't seem to shake.
I'm really worried this could be lymphoma, because my close friend had these exact same drenching night sweats before her diagnosis.
I'm hoping to get some strong antibiotics and have my blood checked so I can get rid of this fever before the weekend.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any chronic medical illnesses like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I had an appendectomy when I was nineteen, but no other surgeries or hospital stays since then.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or vitamins.
I don't have any known allergies to antibiotics or other medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only have a glass of beer once or twice a month socially.
I work part-time at a local convenience store and live in an apartment with my partner.
There is no history of early heart disease, rheumatic fever, or immune disorders in my family.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, and my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days.
We use condoms regularly, and there is no chance that I could be pregnant right now.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 38.9°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air.
Mild conjunctival pallor; no subconjunctival petechiae, hemorrhages, or scleral icterus observed.
Tympanic membranes are pearly grey and intact bilaterally without erythema or effusion.
Pharynx is pink and moist without erythema, exudates, or petechiae; dentition shows no gross caries or abscess.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Tachycardic, regular rhythm with a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur audible at the left lower sternal border that slightly accentuates on inspiration.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender throughout with no rebound tenderness or guarding.
The spleen tip is palpable approximately 1 cm below the left costal margin; liver edge is non-palpable and smooth.
No costovertebral angle tenderness bilaterally on direct percussion.
Linear needle puncture track marks and mild healed scarring noted along both antecubital veins; no Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages, or diffuse petechiae.
Neck is supple with full passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
